query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In corrosion‐resistant steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, a self-healing, chromium‐rich passive film (mainly Cr2O3) forms and is continuously renewed by Cr atoms diffusing along a fine-grained, high-density grain-boundary network. This dynamic oxide layer is the primary mechanism protecting the steel from aggressive species.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional stainless or duplex steels with standard Cr levels and a typical (coarser) grain structure.
generation.intervention: Modify the steel microstructure via controlled heat treatments to refine grains and adjust the Cr concentration through alloying, thereby enhancing the density of grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Exposure to simulated aggressive environments representative of chemical-processing and nuclear-power settings—elevated temperatures, humid and chloride-containing media or molten salts—where oxide formation is thermodynamically favored.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure with increased grain-boundary density that promotes rapid Cr diffusion to the surface.
generation.mechanism: The grain boundaries act as fast diffusion pathways for Cr from the interior, enabling the constant formation and repair of a protective Cr2O3 passive film. This self-healing layer prevents the dissolution and subsequent degradation of the underlying metal in aggressive environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steels with refined grains and optimized Cr content will show thicker, more uniform Cr2O3 layers and reduced corrosion rates compared to their coarse-grained or lower-Cr counterparts when exposed to aggressive corrosive conditions.
generation.baseline: Steels with conventional grain sizes and standard Cr levels, which exhibit moderate passive film stability and higher corrosion rates under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic protection is expected to hold in environments where oxidation is favored (moderate to high temperatures with sufficient oxygen) and provided that a minimum Cr content (typically above ~10-12 wt%) is maintained. Extreme conditions that alter oxide thermodynamics or if the steel composition falls below the critical Cr threshold might invalidate this mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: While the protective role of Cr2O3 is well known, the quantitative impact of grain-boundary-mediated Cr diffusion on passive film stability under dynamic, high-temperature corrosive conditions requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel samples with identical nominal compositions but different microstructures: one set with a fine-grained structure (high grain-boundary density) and one with a coarse-grained structure. Additionally, prepare a variant with deliberately reduced Cr content. Expose all samples to a simulated nuclear/chemical-processing environment (e.g., high-temperature, chloride-containing solution or molten salt) and perform time-resolved monitoring of corrosion behavior along with surface analysis.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess passive film integrity
Weight-loss measurements to quantify corrosion rate
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to analyze surface film composition and thickness (focusing on Cr2O3 content)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fine-grained, high-Cr samples do not show significantly enhanced formation or stability of the Cr2O3 passive layer and correspondingly lower corrosion rates compared to the coarse-grained or low-Cr variants, then the role of grain-boundary-facilitated Cr diffusion in sustaining corrosion resistance would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Early research reported that stainless steel, Fe-Cr alloy, and CrFe15Ni15 alloy have excellent corrosion resistance due to the dense Cr2O3 passivation film formed on the surface [,,]. Similarly, it was speculated that the Cr2O3 passivation film has the same effect in the corrosion resistance of HEAs. AlCoCrFeNi [], AlxCrFe1.5MnNi0.5 [], and Al0.5CoCrCuFeNiBx [] verified the foregoing speculation. Therefore, for the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating passivation film of this study, it can be obtained from the results of XPS that the Cr2O3 in the passivation film provides good corrosion resistance for the coating, and the addition of trace amount of Nb results in forming a stable metal oxide of Nb2O5 in the passivation film of the coating, which also plays a positive role in the corrosion resistance [,].

Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy. Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion.

cited_evidence.kind: web:4.1. Effect of Alloy Composition on Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior
cited_evidence.text: Cr depletion depth increased significantly in DS2205 compared to AlCoCrFeNi2.1, with an increase in temperature from 450 °C to 650 °C. At 650 °C, the Cr depletion depth for AlCoCrFeNi2.1 was ~50 μm, while that for DS2205 was ~300 μm. This suggests that Al in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 acted as a sacrificial element and reduced Cr dissolution rate in the molten salt compared to DS2205. Redox control technique has been utilized for corrosion mitigation in molten fluoride and chloride salts []. Dissolution of Al and Cr into the molten salt resulted in the formation of AlCl3 and CrCl2, which formed a redox couple of Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2. At the redox potential, Co, Ni, and Fe become relatively nobler and their dissolution is thermodynamically unfavorable. These findings suggest that Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2 couple may be used as redox buffer to slow or stop the dissolution of Fe, Co, and Ni from AlCoCrFeNi2.1 [].
